parole.significato: Productive suffix giving an adjective a nounal meaning; -ness, -ity
parole.testo: From Old Swedish -het, which is borrowed from Middle Low German -heit, from Proto-Germanic *haiduz. Cognate with Danish -hed, German -heit, Dutch -heid, English -hood.

parole.significato: stern (the rear part or after end of a ship or vessel)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German achter, from Old Saxon aftar, from Proto-Germanic *after. Cognate with Swedish efter, Dutch achter, English after.

parole.significato: to work, to be employed to do
parole.testo: From Old Swedish arbeida, arbeta, from Middle Low German arbeiden (“to work”), from Old Saxon arvēdian (“to offer”), from Proto-Germanic *arbaidijaną, from *arbaidiz (“labour, work, toil, hardship, suffering”), equivalent of arbete + -a. Compare Norwegian arbeide, Norwegian Nynorsk arbeide, arbeida,
From Old Swedish art, from Middle Low German art, from Old Saxon *ard, from Proto-Germanic *ardiz (“character, nature, inborn quality”).

Borrowed from Middle Low German barsch, from Old Saxon *barsk, from Proto-Germanic *barskaz, from *barsaz (“perch, bass”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰórs-o-s, from *bʰers- (“top, tip, point”). Related to borst, borste, -borre (in abborre, sjöborre and kardborre), (possibly) barr (as in granbarr), b
Derived from Middle Low German bedroven, from Proto-Germanic *drōbijaną. Cognate of Danish bedrøve, Dutch bedroeven, German betrüben.

parole.significato: to bury; to perform a burial
parole.testo: From Old Swedish begrava, from Middle Low German begrāven, from Proto-Germanic *bigrabaną. Equivalent to be- + gräva.

From Middle Low German beginnen, from Old Saxon biginnan, from Proto-Germanic *biginnaną. Compare Danish begynde, Norwegian Bokmål begynne, Norwegian Nynorsk begynne, begynna, Low German begünnen, North Frisian begin, Saterland Frisian beginne, West Frisian begjinne, Scots begin, English begin, Dutc
From Middle Low German bekomen, from Old Saxon biqueman, bikuman, from Proto-Germanic *bikwemaną. Equivalent to be- + komma.
From Old Swedish berøma, from Middle Low German berômen, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bi- + *hrōmiz (“fame, glory”). Compare German berühmen. Related to rosa (“to praise, to commend”).

From Old Swedish beroren, from Middle Low German beroren, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bi- (“be-”), *hrōzijaną (“to stir”), equivalent to be- + röra. Cognate with Danish berøre, Norwegian Bokmål berøre, German berühren and Dutch beroeren.

Inherited from Old Swedish berøva, from Middle Low German beroven, from Proto-Germanic *biraubōną. By surface analysis, be- + röva. Cognate of Danish berøve, Gothic 𐌱𐌹𐍂𐌰𐌿𐌱𐍉𐌽 (biraubōn), Dutch beroven, English bereave.

From Old Swedish besitia, from Middle Low German besitten, from Proto-Germanic *bisitjaną, from *bi- + *sitjaną. Equivalent to be- + sitta. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål besitte, Danish besidde, Dutch bezitten, German besitzen, English besit and Gothic 𐌱𐌹𐍃𐌹𐍄𐌰𐌽 (bisitan).

From Old Swedish bevara, from Middle Low German bewaren, from Proto-Germanic *biwarōną from *bi- + *warōną. Equivalent to be- + vara (“to last”). Cognate with English beware, Danish bevare, Norwegian Bokmål bevare, Norwegian Nynorsk bevare, bevara, Dutch bewaren and German bewahren. Displaced native

parole.significato: a criminal, chiefly a thief or robber
parole.testo: From Old Swedish bōve, from Middle Low German bōve, from Proto-Germanic *bō-.
Borrowed from Middle Low German brok, equivalent to German Bruch, from Proto-Germanic *brukiz. Cognate of English breach.

parole.significato: a bulge, a bump (small, round, hard, tender swelling, especially one caused by a strike or blow)
parole.testo: Likely from Middle Low German būle, from Proto-Germanic *būlō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“to blow, inflate, swell up”). Doublet of ballong, boll, bolster, bulle, bälg, and bölja, and probably böld. Compare Norwegian Nynorsk bule and bole, Dutch buil, German Beule, English boil.

parole.significato: a bundle, a bunch (often of broad and flat or long and narrow objects, for example a stack of paper)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German bunt, from Old Saxon *bund, from Proto-Germanic *bundą.

parole.significato: a (usually plastic) container shaped somewhat like a jerry can
parole.testo: From Middle Low German tunneke, a diminutive of tunne (“barrel”), from Proto-Germanic *tunnǭ, *tunnō (“tun, barrel, cask”), from Latin tunna.
From Middle Low German dunst, from Old Saxon *dunst, from Proto-Germanic *dunstą. Cognate of German Dunst.
From Old Swedish dämpa, from Middle Low German dempen, from Proto-Germanic *dampijaną.

From Old Swedish enkil, from Middle Low German enkel, from Proto-Germanic *ainkila-, equivalent to en (“one”) + -el. Compare etymology of English simple. Cognate with Danish enkel, enkelt, Norwegian enkel, Icelandic ekkil, Dutch enkel and Gothic 𐌰𐌹𐌽𐌰𐌺𐌻𐍃 (ainakls). Compare also Latin singulus with th
From Middle Low German vāre, vār, from Old Saxon *fāra, fār, from Proto-Germanic *fērō (“danger”), whence Old English fær, Old Norse fár, German Gefahr.

From Old Swedish föghia, fögha; from Middle Low German vôgen, from Old Saxon fōgian, from Proto-Germanic *fōgijaną. Cognate with Dutch voegen, Old High German fuogen (“to add”) (German fügen), Old English fēġan (English fay). Doublet of fager, föga, få, and fånga.

parole.significato: religious in a quiet and serious way, pious
parole.testo: From Old Swedish fromber, from Middle Low German vrome, from Old Saxon fruma, from Proto-Germanic *frumô, related to Dutch vroom (“pious”).

parole.significato: colour; the spectral composition of visible light
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish færgha, from Middle Low German verwe or varwe, from Proto-Germanic *farwō. Cognate with German Farbe, Danish farve, Dutch verf and Norwegian farge.
From Old Swedish forfæra, from Middle Low German vorvēren, vorvāren, related to fara (“danger”), from Old Saxon *fāra, fār, from Proto-Germanic *fērō (“danger”). Cognate of Norwegian Bokmål forferde.

From Old Swedish forlata, from Middle Low German vorlaten (“to leave”), from Proto-Germanic *fralētaną, equivalent to för- + låta. Cognate with Danish forlade, German verlassen, Gothic 𐍆𐍂𐌰𐌻𐌴𐍄𐌰𐌽 (fralētan), English forlet

parole.significato: to eat or drink, to consume
parole.testo: From Old Swedish fortæra, from Middle Low German vorteren (cognate of German verzehren). Equivalent to för- + tära (cognate with English tear), from Proto-Germanic *teraną.

parole.significato: a journeyman (tradesman who has served an apprenticeship)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German geselle, from Old Saxon gisellio, from Proto-Germanic *gasaljô.
From Old Swedish grus, from Middle Low German grus, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *greutą (“grit”).

parole.significato: mine (place from which ore is extracted)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German grôve, from Proto-Germanic *grōbō (“groove, furrow”). The modern sense is a semantic loan from German Grube, from the same Germanic etymon.
From Middle Low German hantwerk from Proto-Germanic *handuwerką; equivalent to hand (“hand”) + verk (“work”). Cognate with Dutch handwerk, German Handwerk, English handwork.

Borrowed from Middle Low German herkomst, herkumpst. Compare similarly borrowed ankomst (“arrival”) and tillkomst (“coming into existence, creation”). The second element -komst is from Proto-Germanic *kumþiz, but is not a native Swedish formation, rather a borrowing of the Middle Low German suffix.
Borrowed from Middle Low German, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *kīnaną (“to split, crack open”).
From Old Swedish klinga, from Middle Low German klingen, from Old Saxon klingen, from Proto-Germanic *klinganą. Cognate with English clink.

parole.significato: a solid (large) ball, often harder than a boll
parole.testo: From Old Swedish klōt, from Middle Low German klôt, from Old Saxon *klōt, from Proto-Germanic *klautaz. Cognate of German Kloß, English cleat, Dutch kloot. Compare with origin for klut.
Borrowed from Middle Low German klumpe, from Old Saxon *klumpo, from Proto-Germanic *klumpô.

parole.significato: to pinch, to squeeze (often two body parts against each other)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German knīpen, from Proto-Germanic *knīpaną (“to pinch”).
From Middle Low German knōp (“knot”), probably via Old Saxon from a variant of Proto-Germanic *knappô (“knob, lump”), one of several kn- words related to *knuttô (“knot”). Compare Dutch knoop.

Inherited from Old Swedish kora, from Middle Low German koren. Cognate of Norwegian Bokmål kåre. From Proto-Germanic *kuzą, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵews-. Compare origin of kurfurste, tjusa, villkor.
From Middle Low German krampe (whence Norwegian krampe and Danish krampe), from Old Saxon krampo, from Proto-Germanic *krampō, from Proto-Indo-European *grem-.

parole.significato: a (more rustic) premise where alcohol is sold and consumed; a pub, (except often not as strong in tone) a tavern
parole.testo: From Old Swedish krogher, from Middle Low German krôch, from Proto-Germanic *kranhō (“corner”), which according to Kroonen could be related to *kringaną (“to turn, yield”). However, it could otherwise be from Proto-Germanic *kragan- (“throat”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *gʷrogʰ-, which could

Inherited from Old Swedish krusa, from Middle Low German krûsen, related with Proto-Germanic *kruzlǭ (“bent or crooked object, curl”). Further origin uncertain. Possibly from Pre-Germanic *grus-, contracted from Proto-Indo-European *gurus- (“twist, curl”), same source as Persian گرس (gors, “braid of

Inherited from Old Swedish lindormber, from Middle Low German lindworm, from Proto-Germanic *linþawurmiz. Cognate of Old Norse linnormr. By surface analysis, a compound of orm (“serpent”) and a word of disputed origin, arguably meaning "soft" or "pliable". Compare Old Norse linnr (“snake, serpent”)
From Middle Low German lûtteren, from Proto-Germanic *hlūtraz. Literal sense attested since 1541, figurative sense attested since 1756. Cognate of German läutern, Danish luttre, Norwegian luttre.

Borrowed from Middle Low German lucke, gelucke. According to the OED, it may be related to the source of English lock (compare Proto-Germanic *lūkaną (“to close, to shut”)). Compare Danish and Norwegian Bokmål lykke, and Norwegian Nynorsk lukke f. Compare also English luck, German Glück, Yiddish גלי

Known from Old Swedish midhel, middel, medhel, from Middle Low German middel, from Old Saxon middil, from Proto-Germanic *midlą. Same as German Mittel and English middle. The stand-alone adjective is archaic, but lives on as the superlative medelst, as a prefix medel- and many related words, e.g. em

parole.significato: to mean; to convey, or to want to convey
parole.testo: From Old Swedish mena, from Middle Low German mēnen, meinen (compare Icelandic meina, Danish mene), from Old Saxon mēnian, from Proto-Germanic *mainijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *mein-.
From Old Swedish mata f, mate m, from Middle Low German māte, from Old Saxon metan, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *metaną.

parole.significato: to direct, to aim (often of a punch or other aggressive act)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish mata, from Middle Low German māten, from Old Saxon metan, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *metaną.

parole.significato: a bag; an unpleasant older woman
parole.testo: From Middle Low German pack, packe, of uncertain ultimate origin, but possibly from a group of words related to Proto-Germanic *pakkô (“pack”).

parole.significato: potty: small, usually plastic, chamber pot used as toilet for small children
parole.testo: Derived from Middle Low German pot, from Proto-Germanic *puttaz (“pot, jar, tub”). Doublet of pott.
From Middle Low German pricken, from Old Saxon *prikkian, from the verb Proto-Germanic *prikjaną (“to prick”).

parole.significato: a long, thin (often flexible) piece used in some construction, for example a lath
parole.testo: Derived from Middle Low German ribbe, from Proto-Germanic *ribją, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rebʰ-. Doublet of revben. Cognate of German Rippe, English rib.

From Old Swedish ringa, from Middle Low German ringe, from Old Saxon (gi)ringi (“light”), from Proto-Germanic *ga- + *reng-ja, of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Indo-European *wrengʷʰ- (“to squeeze, wring”) and cognate with Proto-Germanic *wringaną (“to squeeze, wring”), Ancient Greek ῥίμ

parole.significato: to save (prevent from dying or going under more broadly, like in English)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish rædda, from Middle Low German redden, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hradjaną. Cognate with Danish redde. First attested in the early 14th century.

parole.significato: rat; an omnivorous rodent of the genus Rattus.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish rotta, from Middle Low German rotte, from Proto-Germanic *rattō.

parole.significato: visibility (ability to see long distances, contingent on fogginess, obstacles, etc.)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German sicht, from Proto-Germanic *sihti. See German Sicht for more.
From Old Swedish skōpa, borrowing from Middle Low German schōpe, from Proto-Germanic *skōpō.
From Old Swedish skænkia, from Middle Low German schenken, from Old Saxon skenkian, from Proto-Germanic *skankijaną.
From Old Swedish slember, from Middle Low German slim, from Proto-Germanic *slimbaz. Related to German schlimm (“bad”).
From Middle Low German slicken, from Proto-Germanic *slikkōną.

parole.significato: snake, slither, wind (move in a winding manner)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German slingeren, from Proto-Germanic *slingwaną.

parole.significato: a castle, a palace (large, grand building serving or previously serving as a residence for royalty or nobility (where f…
parole.testo: From Middle Low German slot, from Proto-Germanic *slutą (see Proto-West Germanic *slot for more).

Borrowed from Middle Low German slû, probably from a Proto-Germanic *slūhaz (“sneaking, creeping”), perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)leuǵ (“to crawl, slide”), if the original sense referred to sneaking and sliding. Cognate of German schlau, Dutch sluw, Norwegian slu.

parole.significato: an ill-mannered boy or young man; a punk, a brat
parole.testo: Derived from Middle Low German slungel. Cognate of German Schlingel (obsolete form Schlüngel). Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *slingwaną. Compare origin of slunga and slänga.
From Old Swedish slækt, borrowed from Middle Low German slecht (“family, lineage”), from Proto-Germanic *slahtō, from the verb *slahaną.
Borrowed from Middle Low German smecker, from Proto-Germanic *smikraz. Cognate of Old English smicer.
Borrowed from Middle Low German smēden, smāden, from Proto-Germanic *smēhijaną (“belittle”). Compare origin of försmå, Dutch smaad and German schmähen.
Borrowed from Middle Low German smechten, smachten, from Proto-Germanic *smēhaz. Cognate of German schmachten, Dutch smachten, Danish smægte.

parole.significato: to snatch, to snap (take with a short, quick motion, literally or figuratively)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German snappen (“speak rapidly”), which is probably related to snavel (“beak, snout”), from Old Saxon *snavel, from Proto-Germanic *snabulaz. Cognate of German schnappen, Dutch snappen. Compare origin of snopen.

parole.significato: a bird in the Scolopacidae family
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German sneppe, after the long, thin beak of the bird, from or related to Old Saxon *snabul, from Proto-Germanic *snabulaz (“snout, beak, mouth”). Cognate of German Schnepfe, Dutch snip, Faroese mýrisnípa. First attested in 1664.
Borrowed from Middle Low German spitze, from Proto-Germanic *spitjaz. Compare German Spitze.

parole.significato: to distribute, to spread, to disseminate
parole.testo: From Old Swedish spridha, probably the same word as spredha, from Middle Low German sprēden, spreiden, from Proto-Germanic *spraidijaną (“to spread”). Cognate with English spread and German spreiten. Due to the absence of this word in Old Icelandic, the Swedish word as well as Danish sprede, Norwegi

parole.significato: stiff; unbending, which does not easily fold
parole.testo: Used in Old Swedish. Cognate with Old Danish and Middle Low German stif, related to Latin stipes (pole, beam). The second meaning (skilled) used since 1614. From Middle Low German stīf, from Old Saxon *stīf, from Proto-Germanic *stīfaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *steyp.

From a verb meaning "to move things around," from or cognate Middle Low German stûken (“to push, bump, compress”), from Old Saxon *stūkan, from Proto-Germanic *stūkaną (“to be stiff, push”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewg- (“to pound, push, beat”). By surface analysis, stök + -a. Possibly related

From Old Swedish svavel, from Middle Low German swavel, swevel, from Old Saxon sweval, from Proto-Germanic *sweblaz. Cognate of German Schwefel, Dutch zwavel, Danish svovl, Old English swefl, Gothic 𐍃𐍅𐌹𐌱𐌻𐍃 (swibls).
From Middle Low German swimen, from Proto-Germanic *swīmaną (“to sway, to swoon”). Cf. Danish and Norwegian Bokmål besvime, Norwegian Nynorsk svima av, English sweem, Dutch zwijm.

parole.significato: to float (in the air), to hover, to soar
parole.testo: From Old Swedish svæva‚ likely borrowed from Middle Low German swēven, from Old Saxon *swivian, from Proto-Germanic *swibāną. Doublet of sviva.

parole.significato: a brother-in-law; a brother of someone's spouse
parole.testo: * The SAOB dictionary states that this is inherited from Old Swedish svāgher, swoger. * From Middle Low German swāger, from Old Saxon *swāgar, from Proto-Germanic *swēgraz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱuros (“husband's father”).

parole.significato: jam (sweet mixture of fruit boiled with sugar, usually with a fairly loose consistency – compare marmelad)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German sulten, from Old Saxon *sultia, from Proto-Germanic *sultijō.

From Old Swedish sælle (“a companion”), from Middle Low German selle, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *saljô (“a roommate”). Related to sal (“a large room, a hall”). Cognate with Danish and Norwegian selle.
From Middle Low German seltsam (“rare”), from Proto-Germanic *seldanē. First part is the same root as in sällan and sällsynt. Compare Dutch zeldzaam, Danish sælsom.

From Old Swedish þanke, borrowed from Middle Low German danke, from Old Saxon thanc, from Proto-Germanic *þankaz, with the initial consonant of the related verb Swedish tänka (“think”). The Middle Low German word has also been borrowed to Danish tanke, Norwegian tanke, and Icelandic þanki.

parole.significato: to tumble (fall head over heels), to roll
parole.testo: From Middle Low German tummelen, from Proto-Germanic *tūmōną (“to tumble”).
From Middle Low German twist, from Proto-Germanic *twi-. Compare German Zwist. See also tvedräkt.
From Middle Low German wachte, from Old Saxon wahta, from Proto-Germanic *wahtwō.
Inherited from Old Swedish vara, from Middle Low German waren, from Old Saxon waron, from Proto-Germanic *warōną. Cognate with Danish vare.
From Old Swedish vinka, from Middle Low German winken, from Proto-Germanic *winkōną.

parole.significato: to practice, to train to do something, to exercise
parole.testo: From Middle Low German ȫven, from Old Saxon ōbian, from Proto-Germanic *ōbijaną (“to do, practice”), see also German üben (“to practice”).
